flashcards.q: What is an anaemic domain model and why does layered architecture produce it?
flashcards.a: Domain objects that are pure getters/setters with all business logic in service classes. Layered architecture organizes bands but doesn't enforce dependency direction within them, so this is the path of least resistance under deadline pressure.

flashcards.q: What's the real difference between hexagonal, onion, and clean architecture?
flashcards.a: Same idea (Cockburn 2005, Palermo 2008, Martin 2012): dependencies point inward toward the domain, infra implements interfaces the domain defines. Differences are vocabulary (port/adapter vs entity/use case) not substance.

flashcards.q: What is the core rule all three ports-and-adapters-style architectures enforce?
flashcards.a: Source-code dependencies point toward the domain, never outward. Where control needs to flow outward (e.g. save to DB), the domain defines an interface and an outer layer implements it (dependency inversion).

flashcards.q: What three properties make a module boundary 'real' in a modular monolith?
flashcards.a: No shared tables across modules, no reaching into another module's internal classes, and enforcement by tooling (fitness functions like ArchUnit/import-linter) rather than convention.

flashcards.q: What is the recommended 2026 default starting architecture for most teams?
flashcards.a: The modular monolith: one deployable unit with enforced internal module boundaries, giving most of microservices' organizational clarity without the operational cost.

flashcards.q: What does 2026 industry data show about microservices adoption trends?
flashcards.a: 42% of organizations that adopted microservices have consolidated some services back into larger units; microservices satisfaction down 19 percentage points vs 2024; infra costs reported 3.75x-6x higher for equivalent functionality.

flashcards.q: Name two real costs of microservices that are easy to underestimate.
flashcards.a: Distributed data (cross-service consistency now needs sagas/eventual consistency instead of a DB transaction), and operational multiplication (N services = N deploy pipelines, N dashboards, N on-call surfaces).
A system with the network-call cost of microservices but without independent deployability, usually because services share a database or have contracts so tightly coupled they must release together.

flashcards.q: State Conway's Law and its practical design implication.
flashcards.a: (1967) Systems mirror the communication structure of the organizations that build them. Practical implication: a service boundary that cuts against how teams actually communicate will be fought continuously regardless of the diagram.

flashcards.q: What is the Inverse Conway Maneuver?
flashcards.a: Deliberately restructuring teams to match the target architecture, since it's cheaper to move team boundaries than to hold a service boundary against the grain of actual communication patterns.

flashcards.q: Why is splitting services along technical layers (auth service, validation service, DB service) usually wrong?
flashcards.a: It produces chattiness rather than independence: a single business operation now fans out across N network hops for what used to be N in-process function calls. Split along bounded contexts/business capabilities instead.

flashcards.q: What is the strangler fig pattern for service extraction?
flashcards.a: Introduce a routing layer, incrementally route growing traffic to the new service while the old code path stays live, cut over once proven, then delete the old path. System is releasable at every step, unlike a big-bang rewrite.

flashcards.q: When is splitting into a separate microservice actually justified?
flashcards.a: A named forcing function: a component with a genuinely different scaling profile, a measured deployment-cadence bottleneck from shared releases, or a real compliance/security isolation requirement -- not 'microservices are what serious companies do.'

flashcards.q: When should you NOT use hexagonal/onion/clean architecture?
flashcards.a: When the app has one datastore that will never realistically change and the domain logic is thin -- the extra ports/adapters/use-case indirection costs more than it saves for a simple CRUD app.
